reason: Paris depended on the Seine and its tributaries for grain, wine, wood and sea imports via Rouen throughout the period.

sea_head.evidence: Rouen was the Seine's seaport where sea-going ships unloaded for transfer to river boats to Paris.

river_head.evidence: Paris river merchants (the marchands de l'eau / Hanse parisienne) controlled Seine traffic between Paris and the lower river.

head.place: Compiegne/Noyon (nearest tag noyon; Compiegne has no tag)
head.evidence: The Oise carried Picard grain and goods down to the Seine and Paris.
Marne boats brought Champagne grain and wine down to Paris.
Auxerre and lower Burgundy wines went to Paris by boat on the Yonne.

obstacles.name: Pertuis de Poses / Pont-de-l'Arche shallows (nearest tag louviers)
obstacles.evidence: Upstream boats needed hauling through the shallow mill-weir passage near Poses and Pont-de-l'Arche before 19th-century canalisation.

period_note: Continuous through 1300-1837; tidal estuary below Rouen (mouth near Harfleur/Honfleur, nearest tag tancarville).

reason: The Loire was France's busiest inland waterway, carrying salt, wine and goods between Nantes and Orleans with an organised merchants' community.

sea_head.evidence: Nantes was the Loire's sea port; larger ships later stopped lower at Paimboeuf.

river_head.evidence: Orleans was the trade hub where the Loire came closest to Paris and headquarters of the Loire boatmen-merchants' community.

obstacles.name: Sandbanks and summer low water (e.g. around Tours/Saumur)
obstacles.evidence: Shifting sandbanks and low summer flow made Loire navigation seasonal and slow.

period_note: Boats also went higher (Roanne) but Orleans was the terminus of bulk trade; Angers on the Maine lies just off the main stem.

reason: The Garonne carried the high-country wine, grain and woad from Toulouse down to Bordeaux's export fleets.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going ships ascend the tidal Garonne to Bordeaux, the wine-fleet port.

river_head.evidence: Medieval boatmen carried goods between Toulouse and Bordeaux; the Toulouse head of traffic lay below the Bazacle weir.

head.place: Montauban (river trade reached Gaillac, which has no tag)
head.evidence: Gaillac wines came down the Tarn to Bordeaux in the Middle Ages.
Cahors wine was shipped down the Lot to Bordeaux.

obstacles.name: Bazacle weir at Toulouse
obstacles.evidence: The Bazacle mill dam ended through-navigation at Toulouse; traffic started below it.

period_note: Navigation seasonal (roughly November-June); never canalised in the period (Canal de Garonne 1850s).

reason: The Dordogne carried Bergerac and Perigord wine to Libourne and the Gironde.

sea_head.evidence: Libourne was a tidal wine port reached by sea-going ships at the Dordogne-Isle confluence.

river_head.evidence: Gabarres carried wine from Bergerac down to Libourne; the rapids above Lalinde limited upstream trade.

period_note: Joins the Garonne at Bec d'Ambes to form the Gironde; Libourne was an English-held bastide wine port 1270-1453.

reason: From the Middle Ages the Charente was the main trade route between the Atlantic salt coast and Cognac/Angouleme (salt up, wine/brandy/stone/paper down).

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going ships loaded brandy and wine at Tonnay-Charente; Rochefort arsenal from 1666.

river_head.evidence: Gabarres carried goods between Angouleme, Cognac and the coast; the stretch above Cognac was abandoned only in 1926.

period_note: Canalised only 1772-1835, but boat trade is continuous from the Middle Ages; brandy trade grows after 1600.

reason: The Rhone-Saone axis was the main north-south trade corridor linking the Mediterranean with Lyon, Burgundy and the Champagne/Geneva fairs.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going ships reached Arles; the silting mouths made the lower delta hard for larger ships.

river_head.evidence: Lyon was the great Rhone-Saone river port and fair town; the Rhone above Lyon was barely navigable.

head.evidence: The Saone was an easy, slow waterway; Chalon was its fair town and main river port (boats reached Gray).

obstacles.name: Pont-Saint-Esprit bridge passage (nearest tag viviers)
obstacles.evidence: The fast current through the arches of the medieval bridge at Pont-Saint-Esprit was a notorious hazard.

obstacles.name: Rhone mouth bars (tag arles)
obstacles.evidence: Shifting sand bars at the delta mouths hindered sea ships reaching Arles.

period_note: Upstream traffic needed horse towing against a strong current; Avignon, Beaucaire (fair) and Vienne lie on the reach.

reason: Europe's busiest river route: Rhine wine, metals and Upper German goods to the Low Countries, with staple towns along the way.

sea_head.evidence: Under Cologne's 1259 staple right, deep lower-Rhine/sea craft and shallow upper-Rhine boats transshipped at Cologne.

river_head.evidence: Rhine boat traffic ran up to Basel; the falls and rapids above Basel (Laufenburg, Rhine Falls) ended through-navigation.

head.evidence: The Waal-Merwede arm carried Rhine traffic past Nijmegen to the Dordrecht staple and the sea; branch head is its sea end.
The Main carried goods to the Frankfurt fairs, the river's main trade terminus.
Moselle wine and goods moved by boat between Trier and Koblenz.
Heilbronn held Neckar navigation privileges (1333) and was the head of regular Neckar shipping.

obstacles.name: Middle Rhine gorge reefs: Binger Loch and Lorelei (nearest tag katzenelnbogen, which held St. Goar)
obstacles.evidence: The rock bar at the Binger Loch and the reefs by the Lorelei were the most dangerous passages on the Rhine.

period_note: Staple towns Cologne and Mainz forced transshipment; dozens of tolls. Delta: IJssel listed separately; Lek/Nederrijn omitted as minor.

reason: The Meuse carried Ardennes stone, timber, coal and Dinant/Liege metalwork downstream and salt and fish upstream, with ports at Namur, Huy, Liege and Maastricht.

sea_head.evidence: Dordrecht at the Maas-Merwede junction was the sea-going port and staple for Meuse traffic.

river_head.place: Namur (trade reached Dinant and Mezieres; dinant tag has has_river False)
river_head.evidence: Medieval Meuse ports ran from Mezieres through Dinant, Namur, Huy and Liege to Maastricht.

period_note: Many small-lordship tolls rather than physical barriers; Venlo, Roermond, Maastricht and Liege lie on the reach.

reason: The Scheldt linked Antwerp, Europe's leading 16th-century port, with Ghent and the Tournai stone and Hainaut grain country.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going ships reached Antwerp until the Dutch closed the Scheldt in 1585.

river_head.evidence: Tournai stone and Hainaut grain went downriver to Ghent's grain staple and Antwerp.

head.evidence: The Lys carried Artois grain and Flemish goods to Ghent.
Mechelen's staple for salt, fish and oats relied on boats on the Dijle from the Scheldt/Rupel.

period_note: 1585-1795 the Dutch blocked the Scheldt mouth for sea trade to Antwerp; river traffic continued.

reason: Kept, but merged into the Scheldt entry as a branch (Ghent-Kortrijk).

sea_head.evidence: Ghent sits at the Lys-Scheldt confluence.

period_note: See Scheldt branches.

reason: The IJssel connected the Rhine with the Zuiderzee and carried the trade of the Hanseatic towns Kampen, Zwolle, Deventer, Zutphen and Doesburg.

sea_head.evidence: Kampen was a Hanseatic seaport at the IJssel mouth.

river_head.place: Arnhem (IJssel leaves the Rhine at Westervoort, next to Arnhem)
river_head.evidence: The IJssel is a Rhine branch; Deventer and Zutphen traded with Cologne along it.

obstacles.name: Silting of the IJssel (from c. 1430)
obstacles.evidence: Silting from about 1430 gradually ended Kampen's prosperity.

period_note: Strong in 1300-1450, declining after; deventer and zutphen tags exist but have has_river False. Neither the vanilla map nor the hydrology network draws the IJssel (a Rhine distributary), so its channel runs straight through its stops.

reason: London's grain, malt, wood and wool supply from the Thames valley came by barge.

sea_head.evidence: London was the sea port; sea ships moored below London Bridge.

river_head.evidence: By c.1300 Henley was the main transshipment point for grain to London and effectively the head of large-scale navigation; Burcot/Oxford only reopened c.1600-1635.

obstacles.name: Old London Bridge
obstacles.evidence: The narrow arches of medieval London Bridge made a dangerous fall ('shooting the bridge') and stopped ships going above it.

period_note: Head moved upstream to Burcot then Oxford after the Oxford-Burcot Commission (1605-1635).

reason: The Severn was England's busiest free river, with trows carrying goods between Bristol Channel ports, Gloucester, Worcester, Bewdley and Shrewsbury.

sea_head.evidence: Gloucester was the highest port reached by sea-going vessels on the tidal Severn (customs port from 1580).

river_head.evidence: Severn trows traded up to Shrewsbury; Bewdley (no tag) was a major inland port.

period_note: Bristol (on the Avon, tag bristol) was the regional sea port; the Severn tidal bore and shoals hindered but did not stop trade.

reason: Hull, York and the Trent towns were joined by one river system carrying wool, lead, grain and cloth.

sea_head.evidence: York traded overseas by ship in the 14th century; by the late 16th century larger sea ships could no longer reach it.

head.place: Nottingham (Gainsborough, the Trent's sea-ship port, has no tag)
head.evidence: Gainsborough became the main inland port on the Trent in the 16th century; boats traded on to Nottingham.

obstacles.name: Silting of the Ouse below York
obstacles.evidence: Sediment build-up cut York off from larger ships by the late 16th century.

period_note: Mouth port Hull (tag hull). None of york, nottingham or hull have has_river True in the TSV.

reason: King's Lynn's Hanseatic port fed the Fens: boats served Ely, Cambridge (Stourbridge Fair) and Huntingdon.

sea_head.evidence: King's Lynn was a major medieval port at the Great Ouse mouth.

river_head.evidence: Before 17th-century improvements the Bedford bridge blocked the upper river, so trade stopped around St Ives/Huntingdon.

head.evidence: Cambridge and the Stourbridge Fair were supplied by boat from Lynn along the Cam.

period_note: Optional addition; drop if the English set must stay smaller.

reason: Seville was the only port for the Indies trade (1503-1717) and barges carried wool and oil down from Cordoba.

sea_head.evidence: Ocean ships of the Carrera de Indias sailed up the Guadalquivir to Seville.

river_head.evidence: In medieval times barges navigated from Seville up to Cordoba, carrying bulk wool.

obstacles.name: Sanlucar bar
obstacles.evidence: The sand bar at the river mouth made Sanlucar an outport for heavy cargo by 1500.

obstacles.name: Mill weirs between Seville and Cordoba
obstacles.evidence: Mill weirs damaged barges and hindered navigation.

obstacles.name: Silting of the lower river (16th century)
obstacles.evidence: Silting grew worse in the 16th century and began to halt navigation.

period_note: The Seville-Cordoba barge reach faded during the 16th century; sea traffic moved to Cadiz from 1717.

reason: The Tagus estuary and lower river fed Lisbon with Ribatejo grain, wine and wood; in 1552 about 1,490 riverboats served Lisbon.

sea_head.evidence: Lisbon on the Tagus estuary was the imperial seaport.

river_head.place: Tancos/Abrantes (nearest tag torres_novas; santarem is the next big river port downstream)
river_head.evidence: In the 16th century Tancos was the most important Tagus river port, with boats reaching Abrantes.

period_note: Philip II's 1580s scheme to open the Tagus to Toledo did not last; Spanish Tagus excluded.

reason: Rabelo boats carried Alto Douro wine and goods down to Porto/Gaia for centuries (Gaia staple law 1254).

sea_head.evidence: Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia at the mouth were the seaport and staple.

river_head.evidence: Rabelo boats carried port wine from the Douro valley around Regua to the Gaia cellars.

obstacles.name: Rapids along the gorge (Cachao da Valeira above Regua cleared only in the 1790s)
obstacles.evidence: The rocky Douro gorge made every trip a hazardous downstream run.

period_note: Heavy traffic belongs mostly to the port wine era (after c.1680); low confidence for 1300-1600.

reason: Royal privileges protected Zaragoza boatmen, and barges carried Aragonese grain to Tortosa (e.g. 1354).

sea_head.evidence: Tortosa was the sea-going port near the Ebro mouth.

river_head.evidence: Barges carried grain from Zaragoza to Tortosa; a study covers Ebro navigation 1399-1602.

obstacles.name: Rocky narrows and mill weirs around Mequinenza and Flix
obstacles.evidence: The gorge reaches between Mequinenza and Flix were the difficult part of the Zaragoza-Tortosa run.

period_note: Traffic mostly downstream and seasonal; declined after 1600 (Imperial Canal of Aragon later).

reason: The Po carried Venetian salt and goods to Lombardy and grain back, linking Venice, Ferrara, Cremona, Piacenza and Pavia.

sea_head.place: Po delta, Venetian entry via Chioggia/Brondolo (tag chioggia)
sea_head.evidence: Venetian river traffic reached the Po through the lagoon at Chioggia/Brondolo; sea-going ships did not go up the Po.

river_head.evidence: The Po is navigable from its mouth to Pavia, where the Ticino and navigli lead to Milan.

head.evidence: Mantua's lakes connected to the Po via the navigable Mincio.

period_note: Delta mouths shifted (Porto Viro cut 1604); Ferrara/Venice tolls and wars (e.g. 1313 treaty) affected traffic.

reason: Burchi boats hauled salt and goods from the Venetian lagoon up to Verona, the Adige being a trade road between the Alps and Venice.

sea_head.place: Adige mouth at Brondolo near Chioggia (tag chioggia)
sea_head.evidence: The Adige was navigable from Bronzolo down to Brondolo near Venice.

river_head.evidence: Barges went up from the lagoon to Verona's river customs; above Verona mostly rafts came down from Trentino.

period_note: Legnago on the reach; boat traffic above Verona (to Bronzolo) existed but was mixed with timber rafting, so it is left out.

reason: Rome's river ports received sea cargo at Ripa Grande and boats carrying wine, oil, wood and charcoal from Sabina and Umbria at Ripetta.

sea_head.evidence: Coastal ships came up the Tiber from Fiumicino to Rome's Ripa Grande.

river_head.evidence: Boats brought goods down to Rome's Ripetta port from northern Lazio and southern Umbria.

period_note: Mostly downstream traffic; the Ripetta port building dates from 1704 but the trade is older.

reason: Navicelli boats carried Florence's trade between Pisa/Porto Pisano (later Livorno) and the Porto di Signa.

sea_head.evidence: Pisa was the Arno's sea port (Porto Pisano, later Livorno via the Navicelli canal).

river_head.evidence: Signa was Florence's river port; above it goods went on by mule because of the irregular flow.

period_note: Flow irregular, so shallow-draught boats only; Pontedera and Empoli lie on the reach.

reason: The Weser was a staple-controlled trade route from Bremen via Minden and Hameln to Munden.

sea_head.evidence: Bremen was the Weser seaport (Vegesack outport built later because of silting).

river_head.place: Hann. Munden (nearest tag hofgeismar; Munden has no tag)
river_head.evidence: Munden's 1247 staple right on the Weser/Werra/Fulda made it the transshipment head of Weser shipping.

obstacles.name: Hameln weir ('Hamelner Loch')
obstacles.evidence: Ships had to pass a narrow, dangerous gap in the mill weir at Hameln, where the Munden shippers' monopoly ended.

period_note: Minden (tag minden) also held a grain/timber staple.

reason: The Elbe carried salt, grain and goods between Hamburg, Magdeburg, Saxony and Bohemia.

sea_head.evidence: Hamburg was the Elbe's seaport and maintained the lower channel buoys from 1450.

river_head.place: Dresden (Pirna, the staple for Bohemian goods, has no tag)
river_head.evidence: Hamburg merchants traded upstream to Magdeburg and Dresden; Magdeburg's staple forced transshipment on the way.

head.evidence: Berlin-Colln traded with Hamburg by boat via the Spree, Havel and Elbe.

obstacles.name: Domfelsen rock at Magdeburg
obstacles.evidence: The Domfelsen rock bar in the Elbe at Magdeburg is a long-standing navigation hazard at low water.

period_note: Minimal alternative: stop at Magdeburg (staple). Traffic also continued into Bohemia (Litomerice).

reason: Only Emden at the mouth mattered; the Ems above Leer carried small-craft local traffic only.

sea_head.evidence: Emden was the Ems mouth port.

period_note: Excluded.
